Draft a simple contractor agreement for hiring a freelancer/contractor. I'm hiring [contractor name/role] to do [describe the work]. Details:
- Deliverables: [list]
- Deadline: [date]
- Payment: [amount, schedule — e.g., "50% upfront, 50% on delivery"]
- Work arrangement: independent contractor (not employee)
Include sections for: scope of work, payment terms, deadlines, IP ownership (I own the work product), confidentiality, non-solicitation of my clients (optional), termination clause, and independent contractor status confirmation. Plain English. Include signature lines. Disclaimer that this isn't legal advice and should be reviewed by a lawyer.

I'm a [solopreneur / freelancer / small business owner] in [your industry]. Here are my typical monthly expenses:
[List your expenses — e.g., "Slack subscription, Zoom pro, Adobe CC, co-working membership, Uber rides to client meetings, lunch with prospects, Google Ads, contractor payments, etc."]
Create a categorization system for me that: (1) Groups these into tax-friendly categories (for [your country — e.g., US/UK/Canada] tax purposes), (2) Flags which ones are likely fully deductible, partially deductible, or personal, (3) Suggests a simple tracking system (spreadsheet structure or tool recommendation), (4) Identifies any expenses I might be missing that are common for [my type of business]. Format as a clean table.

Write a monthly financial summary email I can send to [my business partner / investors / advisory board]. Include these sections filled with placeholders:
1. Revenue: [total revenue] vs. [previous month] — [up/down X%]
2. Expenses: [total expenses], top 3 categories
3. Net Profit/Loss: [amount and margin]
4. Key metrics: [2-3 KPIs specific to your business — e.g., MRR, CAC, LTV, project count]
5. Cash position: [bank balance] with [X months runway]
6. Notable wins this month: [placeholder]
7. Challenges / risks: [placeholder]
8. Plan for next month: [placeholder]
Tone: transparent, concise, data-driven. This should take 2 minutes to read.

Write a 3-email payment collection sequence for an overdue invoice.
Invoice details: [amount], [client name], originally due [date], for [service/product delivered].
Email 1 (5 days past due): Friendly reminder. Assume it's an oversight. Attach the invoice again. Suggest easy payment methods.
Email 2 (15 days past due): Firmer tone. Reference the original terms. Mention that continued delay may affect [ongoing work / future service / account standing].
Email 3 (30 days past due): Final notice. State that I'll need to [pause services / involve collections / charge a late fee of X% as per contract]. Still professional — never burn a bridge unnecessarily.
Include subject lines. Tone escalates but never gets hostile.

Write a clear late payment policy document I can attach to contracts and reference in invoice emails. My standard terms: [e.g., "Net 30" / "due upon receipt" / "50% upfront, 50% on completion"]. Include: (1) When invoices are sent and when they're due, (2) Accepted payment methods, (3) Grace period (if any), (4) Late fee structure (suggest a reasonable one if I don't have one — e.g., 1.5% per month), (5) Escalation process — what happens at 15, 30, 60, 90 days overdue, (6) Right to pause work on overdue accounts, (7) Collections process. Firm but professional — the goal is to prevent late payments, not scare people off.

Write a professional payment reminder email to [client name] for invoice #[number] of [amount] that was due on [date]. This is [first / second / third] reminder. Tone should be [friendly nudge / firm but professional / final notice before next steps]. Include the original payment terms and a clear CTA to pay by [new deadline]. If this is a final notice, mention that I may need to pause ongoing work or involve [collections / my accountant].

Create a comprehensive tax preparation checklist for a [solopreneur / freelancer / LLC / S-Corp] in [your country/state]. My business is [describe]. Revenue range: [approximate]. I need a checklist of: (1) All documents I need to gather (organized by category: income, expenses, deductions, investments, etc.), (2) Common deductions I shouldn't forget for [my type of business], (3) Key deadlines for [current tax year], (4) Questions I should ask my accountant, (5) Things to organize throughout the year so tax prep isn't hell next time. Be specific — not "gather receipts" but "gather receipts for: meals with clients, business travel, home office expenses, software subscriptions, etc."

I'm trying to decide between these [tools / vendors / platforms] for [purpose]:
Option A: [name and what you know]
Option B: [name and what you know]
Option C: [name and what you know]
My requirements: [list what matters most — e.g., price, ease of use, integrations, support, scalability, specific features]
My budget: [range]
My technical level: [beginner / intermediate / advanced]
My business context: [team size, current tools, growth stage]
Create a structured comparison including: (1) Feature comparison table, (2) Pricing comparison (including hidden costs), (3) Pros and cons of each, (4) Best for [scenario] ratings, (5) My recommendation with reasoning, (6) Migration/implementation considerations. Be opinionated — I want a clear recommendation, not "it depends."
